scope: All 24 exact graph Teach bodies independently reviewed against each canonical objective, constraints, key and topic prerequisites, and all curriculum exemplars. Every proposed worked result was independently recomputed. No proposal or live-content approval.

records.canonical_constraints: first quadrant; ordered pair (x, y), horizontal first

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Starting at the origin, move $3$ right and $5$ up. Give the final ordered pair.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Horizontal movement gives $x=3$; vertical movement gives $y=5$. Write horizontal first.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A marker is at $(2,4)$. Move it $3$ units upward. Give its new coordinates.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The upward move preserves $x=2$ and adds $3$ to the old height: $4+3=7$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: On a grid, column numbers increase rightward and row numbers upward from zero. Give the ordered pair at column $6$, row $1$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Column is the horizontal coordinate and row is the vertical coordinate, so record $6$ before $1$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A robot leaves $(0,0)$, goes $2$ right, $4$ up, then $3$ more right. Give its final coordinates.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Combine the two horizontal moves, $2+3=5$. The only vertical move is $4$ up.

records.worked_problem: A robot starts at $(4,3)$ and moves five units right and two units up. Give its new coordinates.
records.semantic_reasoning: Covers ordered-pair order, origin, and combining horizontal and vertical movement without exceeding the prerequisite scope.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Starting at (4,3), five right gives x=4+5=9 and two up gives y=3+2=5, so the endpoint is (9,5).

records.canonical_constraints: integer coordinates between -10 and 10; left/down are negative

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Move $4$ left and $3$ up from the origin. Give the ordered pair.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Left makes the horizontal coordinate negative, while up makes the vertical coordinate positive.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A point lies where $x=6$ meets $y=-2$. Give its ordered pair.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The intersection must have horizontal coordinate $6$ and vertical coordinate $-2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner moves $5$ down and $7$ left. Give the point reached from the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Record horizontal movement first: left $7$ gives $x=-7$; down $5$ gives $y=-5$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A marker at $(0,0)$ moves $2$ right, $6$ left, and $8$ down. Give its final coordinates.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The horizontal displacement is $2-6=-4$ and the vertical displacement is $-8$.

records.worked_problem: Give the coordinates of the point six units right and four units down from the origin.
records.semantic_reasoning: Teaches signed horizontal and vertical directions and preserves x-before-y, matching the negative-coordinate scope.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Six right from the origin gives x=6; four down gives y=-4, hence (6,-4).

records.canonical_constraints: one coordinate is always 0 for a point on an axis

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Give the coordinates of the point on the x-axis that is $6$ units left of the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A point on the x-axis has $y = 0$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A point lies on the y-axis $3$ units below the origin. Give its coordinates.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A point on the y-axis has $x = 0$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Give the coordinates of the point on the x-axis that is $4$ units right of the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A point on the x-axis has $y = 0$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A point lies on the y-axis $5$ units above the origin. Give its coordinates.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A point on the y-axis has $x = 0$.

records.worked_problem: A point lies on the y-axis nine units above the origin. Give its coordinates.
records.semantic_reasoning: Distinguishes axis points from quadrant points and explicitly uses zero for the unchanged coordinate.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Nine units above the origin leaves x=0 and gives y=9, hence (0,9) on the y-axis.

records.canonical_constraints: quadrants numbered I-IV counterclockwise; points on an axis are in no quadrant

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify two points with both coordinates nonzero: $A=(-4,-3)$ and $B=(2,5)$. Give A and B. Use codes 1,2,3,4 for quadrants I,II,III,IV; 5 for the x-axis, 6 for the y-axis, and 7 for the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Read the signs of each coordinate. A zero coordinate locates an axis, and two zero coordinates locate the origin. The locations give A=3 and B=1 under the stated code mapping.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: These reflected points have opposite signs in both coordinates: $A=(3,-2)$ and $B=(-3,2)$. Give A and B. Use codes 1,2,3,4 for quadrants I,II,III,IV; 5 for the x-axis, 6 for the y-axis, and 7 for the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Read the signs of each coordinate. A zero coordinate locates an axis, and two zero coordinates locate the origin. The locations give A=4 and B=2 under the stated code mapping.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Distinguish an axis point from the origin: $A=(-5,0)$ and $B=(0,0)$. Give A and B. Use codes 1,2,3,4 for quadrants I,II,III,IV; 5 for the x-axis, 6 for the y-axis, and 7 for the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Read the signs of each coordinate. A zero coordinate locates an axis, and two zero coordinates locate the origin. The locations give A=5 and B=7 under the stated code mapping.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Classify the origin and a point below it: $A=(0,0)$ and $B=(0,-6)$. Give A and B. Use codes 1,2,3,4 for quadrants I,II,III,IV; 5 for the x-axis, 6 for the y-axis, and 7 for the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Read the signs of each coordinate. A zero coordinate locates an axis, and two zero coordinates locate the origin. The locations give A=7 and B=6 under the stated code mapping.

records.worked_problem: State the location of A = (8, -3) and B = (-5, 0).
records.semantic_reasoning: Correctly classifies all four sign combinations and the separate axis cases; it does not assign an axis point to a quadrant.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: For (8,-3), x is positive and y negative, so quadrant IV. For (-5,0), y=0, so the point lies on the x-axis.

records.canonical_constraints: reflections across one axis only; integer coordinates

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Reflect $(3,-5)$ across the $x$-axis. Give the image.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Reflection in the horizontal axis preserves $x$ and changes the sign of $y$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Reflect $(-4,2)$ across the $y$-axis. Give the image.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Reflection in the vertical axis negates the horizontal coordinate and preserves the vertical coordinate.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A point $6$ right and $3$ up is mirrored across the vertical axis. Give the image coordinates.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The mirror moves the point the same horizontal distance to the left, while its height remains $3$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner reflects $(-2,-7)$ across the $x$-axis by changing both signs. Give the correct image.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Only the distance above or below the horizontal axis reverses; the leftward coordinate remains $-2$.

records.worked_problem: Reflect $(7,-4)$ across the y-axis. Give the image.
records.semantic_reasoning: States the coordinate invariant for each axis reflection and handles negative signs directly within the stated coordinate-plane prerequisites.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Reflecting (7,-4) across the y-axis negates x only, producing (-7,-4).

records.canonical_constraints: points share an x- or y-coordinate; distance is a positive integer

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Find the distance between $(-3,2)$ and $(5,2)$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The points share $y=2$; their horizontal separation is $5-(-3)=8$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A lift moves from grid height $-4$ to grid height $3$, keeping $x=2$. How far does it move?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The vertical displacement is $3-(-4)=7$; its magnitude is the distance.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A horizontal segment at height $6$ has endpoints with $x$-coordinates $8$ and $2$. Find its length.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Distance is nonnegative: the right endpoint minus the left endpoint is $8-2=6$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner reports distance $-9$ from $(1,5)$ to $(1,-4)$. Give the correct distance.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The signed change is $-4-5=-9$; its magnitude $9$ is the length.

records.worked_problem: How far apart are $(5,-9)$ and $(5,14)$?
records.semantic_reasoning: Selects the changing coordinate for aligned points and uses absolute difference, covering distances that cross zero.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: The points (5,-9) and (5,14) are vertically aligned; |14-(-9)|=|23|=23.

records.canonical_constraints: single-variable-vs-time stories; segments are clearly rising, flat, or falling

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A distance-time graph is horizontal from $t=2$ to $t=5$. Is the walker standing still, moving at a constant nonzero speed, or speeding up?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A flat segment has zero slope, so the distance is not changing over that interval.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A temperature graph goes downward from left to right. Is the temperature increasing, decreasing, or constant?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The graph falls left to right, so the temperature is decreasing.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A savings-account graph rises steadily from left to right. Is the amount saved increasing, decreasing, or constant?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The graph rises left to right, so the amount saved is increasing.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.answer: traveling at a constant speed (60 km/h, not changing)

options: traveling at a constant speed (60 km/h, not changing)

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A car speed-time graph is flat at $60$ km/h from $t = 1$ to $t = 3$. Is the car stopped, traveling at a constant speed, or speeding up?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A flat segment at $60$ means a constant nonzero speed.

records.worked_problem: A graph shows a car park's occupancy in cars on the vertical axis and the time in hours after opening on the horizontal axis. The graph runs straight from $(0, 12)$ to $(3, 96)$, then straight from $(3, 96)$ to $(5, 96)$, then straight from $(5, 96)$ to $(9, 16)$. Over which interval of hours does the occupancy hold one value?
records.semantic_reasoning: Reads increasing, constant, and decreasing intervals from direction while keeping the interpretation tied to the labeled context.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: The example has equal occupancy values from time 3 through time 5, so that interval is constant.

records.canonical_objective: Read meaning from a point on a graph
records.canonical_constraints: interpret one labeled point or feature; axes always named in the problem

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: On a cost-versus-items graph, $(4,10)$ is shown. Does it mean 4 items cost €10, 10 items cost €4, or each item costs €4?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The point $(4, 10)$ pairs input $4$ with output $10$: $4$ items cost €$10$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.answer: the maximum height the ball reaches

options: the maximum height the ball reaches

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: On a height-versus-time graph of a thrown ball, does the highest point show maximum height, starting height, or landing time?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The highest point of a height graph marks the maximum height.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.answer: after 3 hours, the hiker has walked 12 km

options: after 3 hours, the hiker has walked 12 km
after 12 hours, the hiker has walked 3 km
the hiker walks 4 km per hour

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: On a distance-versus-time graph, $(3, 12)$ is shown. Does it mean after 3 hours the hiker has walked 12 km, after 12 hours the hiker has walked 3 km, or the hiker walks 4 km per hour?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The ordered pair gives time $3$ and distance $12$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A profit graph crosses the horizontal axis. Does that crossing mark break-even, maximum profit, or starting cost?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: On the horizontal axis the profit coordinate is zero.

records.worked_problem: A graph's horizontal axis measures elapsed minutes and its vertical axis measures the height in meters of a rising weather balloon. The marked point is $(9, 250)$. Interpret that point.
records.semantic_reasoning: Interprets a coordinate using the axis quantities and units rather than treating it as an unlabeled ordered pair.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: At the point (9,250), the horizontal coordinate is 9 minutes and the vertical coordinate is 250 metres.

records.canonical_constraints: steeper means faster change; no slope computation required

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Runner A and runner B start together, and A has the steeper distance-time line. Is runner A faster, runner B faster, or is their speed equal?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A steeper line covers more distance in the same time, so runner A is faster.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A graph rises steeply at first and then gently. Was growth faster at the start, in the middle, or at the end?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The steep part rises more per unit of time, so growth was faster at the start.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Account X and account Y start at €0, and X has the steeper line. Which has faster growth: account X, account Y, or equal growth?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The steeper line has the greater rate.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A hiking graph is gentle in the first hour and steeper in the second. Was the hiker faster in the first hour, second hour, or both equally?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The steeper segment has the greater distance per hour.

records.worked_problem: Two runners have straight distance-time graphs starting at the origin, with minutes horizontally and metres vertically on matching scales. At two minutes, runner C has travelled $400$ m and runner D $600$ m. Which is faster?
records.semantic_reasoning: Limits steepness comparison to matching axes and scales, then connects greater vertical change over the same horizontal change to faster change.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Over 2 minutes, D changes 600 m and C changes 400 m; 600/2=300 m/min exceeds 400/2=200 m/min, so D is faster.

records.canonical_constraints: k = y/x; k may be a simple fraction or decimal

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: For $y=kx$, the pair $(4,10)$ is a solution. Find $k$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The equation gives $10=4k$; dividing both sides by $4$ gives $k=5/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A proportional relationship has output $18$ at input $6$. What number multiplies every input to obtain its output?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: One input unit corresponds to $18/6=3$ output units, the same multiplier for all pairs.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A line through the origin passes through $(8,2)$. Determine its constant of proportionality.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: For a line through the origin, $y=kx$. Thus $2=8k$ and $k=1/4$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: The proportional rule $y=2x$ is proposed for a relationship containing $(5,8)$. Replace the multiplier $2$ with the correct constant.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The proposed rule predicts $10$, while the given output is $8$. The corrected multiplier satisfies $5k=8$.

records.worked_problem: The value y is proportional to x, and $y=45$ when $x=9$. Find k.
records.semantic_reasoning: Defines the constant as output divided by a nonzero input, explains why the origin is insufficient, and preserves input/output roles.

records.canonical_constraints: every row gives the same y/x ratio

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A proportional table has rows $(x,y)=(2,5),(4,10),(6,15)$. Find the common multiplier $k$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Each output divided by its input gives the same ratio: $5/2$, $10/4$, and $15/6$ all reduce to $5/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A table lists inputs $3,5$ above outputs $12,20$, respectively. Determine $k$ in $y=kx$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The paired entries give $12/3$ and $20/5$. Both quotients are $4$, so the same multiplier fits both columns.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A proportional table includes $(0,0),(4,1),(12,3)$. Determine its constant without dividing by zero.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The origin supplies no ratio. Use a nonzero input: $1/4$ agrees with the other usable ratio $3/12$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: For table rows $(2,3),(6,9)$, a learner reports $k=2/3$. Correct the multiplier from input $x$ to output $y$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Use output over input: $3/2$ and $9/6$ agree. The learner reversed both ratios.

records.worked_problem: A proportional table contains $(4,18)$, $(8,36)$, and $(12,54)$. Find k.
records.semantic_reasoning: Checks every nonzero row by exact ratios and separately handles a zero-input row, covering the full table criterion.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: 18/4=9/2, 36/8=9/2, and 54/12=9/2, so the shared constant is 9/2=4.5.

records.canonical_constraints: one quantity per one unit of the other; clean division

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Five kilograms cost €20. Find the cost per kilogram in euros.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide the cost by mass: $20/5=4$ euros per kilogram.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A cyclist travels $42$ km in $3$ hours at a constant rate. Find kilometres per hour.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The unit rate is distance divided by time: $42/3=14$ km per hour.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A printer produces $84$ pages in $7$ minutes. Find pages per minute.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide output by elapsed time: $84/7=12$ pages per minute.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A recipe uses $9$ cups of flour for $6$ batches. Find cups per batch.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The flour for one batch is $9/6=3/2$ cups.

records.worked_problem: 5 kilograms of rice cost 11.25 euros. Find the price per kilogram, in euros.
records.semantic_reasoning: Connects the proportionality constant to a context-specific unit rate with correct units and division direction.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: EUR 11.25 divided by 5 kg is EUR 2.25 per kg because 2.25*5=11.25.

records.canonical_objective: Write and use the equation y = kx
records.canonical_constraints: equation form y = kx

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Use the proportional equation $y=(5/2)x$ to find $y$ at $x=6$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The rule multiplies each input by $5/2$, giving $(5/2)6=15$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A proportional rule sends $3$ to $21$. Write its multiplier mentally, then find the output for $8$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: First solve $21=3k$ to get $k=7$. The same rule gives $y=7(8)=56$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: The equation $d=4t$ models distance in kilometres after $t$ hours. Give the numerical distance after half an hour.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Insert $t=1/2$: $d=4(1/2)=2$ kilometres.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: For $y=3x$, a learner adds $3$ to input $5$. Correct the output using the proportional equation.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The coefficient is a multiplier: $y=3(5)=15$; adding would use a different rule.

records.worked_problem: A proportional relationship has equation $y=9x$. Find y when $x=12$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Explains y=kx as multiplication, includes deriving k from a known nonzero pair, and covers zero input without introducing an additive rule.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Substituting x=12 in y=9x gives y=9(12)=108.

records.canonical_objective: Recognize proportionality from tables and graphs
records.canonical_constraints: proportional graphs are straight lines through the origin; tables have constant y/x

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A table has positive inputs: $(2,8)$ and $(5,20)$. Give ratios=(first,second) for the output/input ratios, then proportional=yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Dividing output by its paired input gives r=4 and s=4. A proportional relationship requires these ratios to agree for every nonzero input.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A straight graph includes the origin and the two indicated points: $(2,5)$ and $(6,15)$. Give ratios=(first,second) for the output/input ratios, then proportional=yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Dividing output by its paired input gives r=5/2 and s=5/2. A proportional relationship requires these ratios to agree for every nonzero input.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A table has a nonzero starting offset; inspect its two rows: $(1,5)$ and $(4,11)$. Give ratios=(first,second) for the output/input ratios, then proportional=yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Dividing output by its paired input gives r=5 and s=11/4. A proportional relationship requires these ratios to agree for every nonzero input.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A table crosses from negative to positive inputs: $(-2,3)$ and $(6,-8)$. Give ratios=(first,second) for the output/input ratios, then proportional=yes or no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Dividing output by its paired input gives r=-3/2 and s=-4/3. A proportional relationship requires these ratios to agree for every nonzero input.

records.worked_problem: A table shows $(2,7)$, $(4,14)$, and $(6,20)$. Is it proportional?
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses both necessary representations: a proportional graph is a line through the origin, while a table requires one common ratio for all nonzero inputs and (0,0) for zero input.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: The ratios are 7/2, 14/4=7/2, and 20/6=10/3; since 21/6 differs from 20/6, the table is not proportional.

records.canonical_constraints: find k first, then solve; integer or half-integer answers

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: In $y=kx$, the pair $(4,10)$ is known. Find $y$ when $x=6$.
A proportional table contains $(3,12)$. Find $x$ when $y=18$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The constant is $12/3=4$; solve $18=4x$, giving $x=9/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Eight metres of fabric cost €20. At the same rate, how many metres cost €35?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The cost per metre is $20/8=5/2$. Thus $(5/2)x=35$, giving $x=14$ metres.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A pump fills $15$ L in $6$ minutes at a proportional rate. How many litres does it fill in $9$ minutes?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The rate is $15/6=5/2$ L/min; multiply by $9$ to get $45/2$ L.

records.worked_problem: A recipe uses five cups of flour for eight servings, in direct proportion. How many cups are needed for twenty servings?
records.semantic_reasoning: Covers finding either a new output or a missing input after finding k, and keeps the contextual units in their correct roles.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: Five cups for eight servings gives k=5/8 cup per serving; (5/8)(20)=100/8=25/2=12.5 cups.

records.canonical_objective: Graph y = kx from two points
records.canonical_constraints: always include the origin plus one more lattice point

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: To graph $y=2x$, plot the origin and the point with $x=3$. Give that second point.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The origin satisfies the equation; at $x=3$, $y=2(3)=6$, so the second lattice point is $(3,6)$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Graph $y=x/2$ using the origin and a point with $y=3$. Give the second point.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Solve $3=x/2$, giving $x=6$. Join $(0,0)$ to $(6,3)$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A proportional graph passes through the origin with rate $-3$. Give its lattice point one unit right of the origin.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: A run of $1$ at rate $-3$ gives rise $-3$, hence $(1,-3)$ beside the origin.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner plots the origin and $(2,6)$ for $y=4x$. Keep $x=2$ and correct the second point.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: At $x=2$, the equation requires $y=4(2)=8$; the origin and $(2,8)$ define the graph.

records.worked_problem: To graph $y=7x$, give the origin and the point with $x=2$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses the defining origin and a second lattice point, with valid branches for selecting x or recovering x from y when k is nonzero.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: For y=7x, x=0 gives (0,0), and x=2 gives y=14, so the second point is (2,14).

records.canonical_constraints: k = y/x from any graphed point; fractional k allowed

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: On a straight graph through the origin, a marked point is $5$ horizontal units and $20$ vertical units from the origin. Read $k$ for $y=kx$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The marked point is $(5,20)$, so $5k=20$ and $k=4$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: The $x$-axis uses $2$ units per square and the $y$-axis $3$ units per square. A proportional line passes through a mark $2$ squares right and $1$ square up. Find $k$.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Convert grid counts to coordinates: $x=2(2)=4$ and $y=3(1)=3$. Thus $k=3/4$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A proportional graph has axes input $x$ and output $y$. A marked point projects to $x=6$ and $y=9$. Determine the line's multiplier.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The projections give $(6,9)$. Dividing the vertical coordinate by the horizontal gives $9/6=3/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner reads $k=3$ from a proportional graph's point $(12,4)$ by reversing the axes. Give the corrected constant.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: In $y=kx$, the vertical coordinate is the output: $4=12k$, so $k=1/3$.

records.worked_problem: A straight proportional graph through the origin contains the marked point $(3,6)$. Find its constant of proportionality.
records.semantic_reasoning: Accounts for axis scales before calculating vertical over horizontal and explicitly excludes the origin as a usable ratio point.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: At (3,6), k=6/3=2; both (0,0) and (3,6) satisfy y=2x.

records.canonical_constraints: compare k values; one comparison per problem

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Compare two proportional graphs. A passes through $(2,11)$; B passes through $(3,12)$. Both include the origin. Give rates=(A,B), and faster=yes if A has the greater signed rate, otherwise no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The output/input ratios give a=11/2 and b=4. Compare these signed rates; equal rates produce no greater rate, and negative rates retain their ordering.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A proportional graph and a table are represented by their nonzero points. A passes through $(4,7)$; B passes through $(5,15)$. Both include the origin. Give rates=(A,B), and faster=yes if A has the greater signed rate, otherwise no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The output/input ratios give a=7/4 and b=3. Compare these signed rates; equal rates produce no greater rate, and negative rates retain their ordering.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: The proportional lines coincide; check their unit rates. A passes through $(3,9)$; B passes through $(7,21)$. Both include the origin. Give rates=(A,B), and faster=yes if A has the greater signed rate, otherwise no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The output/input ratios give a=3 and b=3. Compare these signed rates; equal rates produce no greater rate, and negative rates retain their ordering.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Both proportional lines decrease as x increases. A passes through $(2,-3)$; B passes through $(4,-10)$. Both include the origin. Give rates=(A,B), and faster=yes if A has the greater signed rate, otherwise no.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The output/input ratios give a=-3/2 and b=-5/2. Compare these signed rates; equal rates produce no greater rate, and negative rates retain their ordering.

records.worked_problem: Proportional line A passes through the origin and $(3,21)$. Proportional line B passes through the origin and $(4,16)$. Both use the same axis units. Which has the greater unit rate?
records.semantic_reasoning: Compares signed unit rates in matching units, including ties and the ordering of negative rates, matching all exemplar branches.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: A has rate 21/3=7 and B has rate 16/4=4; 7>4, so A has the greater unit rate.

records.canonical_constraints: positive rise and run; reduce fractions

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: On a line graph, a slope triangle goes $4$ squares right and $6$ squares up. Each square is one unit on both axes. Find the slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The vertical change is $6$ and horizontal change is $4$; rise over run is $6/4=3/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Two marks on a rising graph are separated by $8$ horizontal grid intervals and $2$ vertical intervals. Both axes use one unit per interval. Find the slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The rise is $2$ units for a run of $8$, so the slope is $2/8=1/4$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A graph's slope triangle has a horizontal leg of $3$ units and an upward vertical leg of $9$ units. How much does the line rise per horizontal unit?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Divide the $9$-unit rise among the $3$ horizontal units to obtain $3$ units of rise per unit of run.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner uses run over rise for a graph that rises $5$ units while running $2$ units right. Give the correct slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Slope measures vertical change per horizontal change, so the rise $5$ belongs in the numerator and run $2$ in the denominator.

records.worked_problem: A line rises nine units over a run of four units to the right. Find the slope.
records.semantic_reasoning: Defines slope as rise over run, reads both in axis units, and requires fraction reduction within the positive-slope scope.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: A rise of 9 over a rightward run of 4 gives 9/4, already in lowest terms.

records.canonical_objective: Sign of the slope from direction
records.canonical_constraints: downward left-to-right means negative rise

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A graph falls $4$ units as you move $2$ units right. Give its signed slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Falling gives vertical change $-4$; rightward run is $2$, so the slope is $-4/2=-2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: The right end of a graph segment is $6$ units lower than its left end and $8$ units farther right. Find the signed slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Moving left to right changes height by $-6$ over a positive run of $8$, giving $-6/8=-3/4$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Trace a descending line $5$ squares right and $3$ squares down on a unit grid. What signed rise per unit of run does the graph show?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Downward motion makes the rise $-3$. Divide by the rightward run $5$ to keep the falling direction in the sign.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner assigns positive slope to a line descending $9$ units over a rightward run of $3$. Correct the signed slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The magnitude is the quotient $9/3$; the descent makes the signed slope $-3$.

records.worked_problem: A line drops ten units for every four units it runs to the right. Find the slope.
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses a positive rightward run and a negative rise for descent, preventing the common sign error and preserving reduced form.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: A drop of 10 gives rise -10; -10/4=-5/2.

records.canonical_objective: Slope between two graphed lattice points
records.canonical_constraints: lattice points close together; counting, not the formula

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Count grid squares from $(1,1)$ to $(3,4)$ on a line. What is its slope?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Counting gives $2$ squares right and $3$ up; slope is $3/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Starting at a marked point on a grid, follow the line $3$ squares right and $3$ squares down. Find its slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The signed rise is $-3$ and the run is $3$, so slope is $-3/3=-1$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A grid segment joins $(0,-1)$ to $(4,1)$. A learner counts $4$ up and $2$ right. Correct the slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The segment actually goes $4$ squares right and $2$ up, so slope is $2/4=1/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A lattice line passes through $(2,3)$ and $(2,0)$. Is its slope zero or undefined?
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Counting from one point to the other gives no horizontal movement and a nonzero vertical movement; division by zero is undefined.

records.worked_problem: A graphed line passes through $(0,0)$ and $(1,6)$ on a unit grid. Count rise and run to find its slope.
records.semantic_reasoning: Teaches grid counting in a consistent direction and includes the essential horizontal-zero-slope and vertical-undefined distinctions.
records.independent_arithmetic_evidence: From (0,0) to (1,6), run=1 and rise=6, so slope=6/1=6.

records.canonical_constraints: positive integer slopes

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Use the slope formula for the points $(1,2)$ and $(3,8)$.
A table gives $x:-2,1$ and $y:1,7$. Use coordinate differences to find the slope.
The displacement from one point on a line to another is $\langle4,4\rangle$. Use the coordinate differences to find the slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The displacement gives $\Delta x=4$ and $\Delta y=4$, so $m=\Delta y/\Delta x=4/4=1$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner mixes point order in the slope numerator and denominator for $(2,-1)$ and $(5,11)$. Find the correct slope.

records.worked_problem: Find the slope of the line through $(-2,5)$ and $(4,47)$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Uses vertical change over horizontal change with one consistent point order and states the nonzero-run condition.

records.canonical_constraints: watch subtraction of negatives; integer slopes

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Use the slope formula for the points $(-3,-5)$ and $(1,3)$.
A table gives $x:-4,-1$ and $y:2,-4$. Use coordinate differences to find the slope.
A line starts at $A=(-2,-3)$; its displacement to a second point is $\langle4,4\rangle$. Find the slope.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: The second point is $(2,1)$ and the coordinate changes are $\Delta x=4$, $\Delta y=4$. Thus $m=1$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner mixes point order in the slope numerator and denominator for $(-5,-7)$ and $(-2,2)$. Find the correct slope.

records.worked_problem: Find the slope through $(-7,-5)$ and $(-3,11)$.
records.semantic_reasoning: Makes subtraction of negative coordinates explicit, preserves coordinate pairing, and also covers a supplied displacement.

records.canonical_constraints: consistent order in numerator and denominator

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Use the slope formula for the points $(1,3)$ and $(4,9)$. Compute in both point orders.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: $m=(9-(3))/(4-(1))=(6)/(3)=2$. Reversing both orders gives $(3-(9))/(1-(4))=(-6)/(-3)$, the same ratio because both signs reverse.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A table gives $x:-2,2$ and $y:5,-3$. Use coordinate differences to find the slope. Compute in both point orders.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: $m=(-3-(5))/(2-(-2))=(-8)/(4)=-2$. Reversing both orders gives $(5-(-3))/(-2-(2))=(8)/(-4)$, the same ratio because both signs reverse.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: Two correct orderings for one line give slope quotients $3/6$ and $(-3)/(-6)$. Give their common value.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: Reversing point order negates both coordinate differences. Both quotients reduce to $1/2$.

curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.problem: A learner mixes point order in the slope numerator and denominator for $(-3,-4)$ and $(1,8)$. Find the correct slope. Compute in both point orders.
curriculum_exemplars_reviewed.solution_sketch: $m=(8-(-4))/(1-(-3))=(12)/(4)=3$. Reversing both orders gives $(-4-(8))/(-3-(1))=(-12)/(-4)$, the same ratio because both signs reverse.

records.worked_problem: Find the slope through $(2,-1)$ and $(8,5)$ using both point orders.
records.semantic_reasoning: Explains why either complete point order is valid and why mixing orders is invalid: reversing both differences negates numerator and denominator together.

limitations: Semantic review only. Production gates were outside this review; no proposal files or live content were modified.
